strengths: Elegant and mathematically intuitive formulation: Shifting from simple linear scale-and-shift to higher-order polynomial fitting allows the model to perform non-uniform, depth-dependent corrections. This addresses a real-world limitation of MDE models where relative depth ordering between different regions or objects is misaligned.

First-derivative regularization: The introduction of the monotonicity regularization term ($|1 - \frac{d\hat{d}}{dz}|_1$) is highly principled. It successfully constrains the flexible polynomial function space, preventing oscillatory behavior and ensuring that the relative structural ordering of the MDE model is preserved locally.

Significant performance improvements: PolyRad achieves state-of-the-art results on three major radar-camera datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft), outperforming existing baselines by very large margins (e.g., up to 54.6% in MAE on ZJU).

Thorough evaluation: The paper conducts rigorous evaluations using multiple MDE backbones (DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, UniDepth), provides comprehensive ablation studies of each architectural component, and performs sensitivity analysis on the polynomial degree hyperparameter.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter sensitivity: The choice of the polynomial degree $N$ is treated as a global hyperparameter. Although analyzed in Table 3, the optimal degree might vary under different scene conditions, and a method to adaptively or dynamically determine $N$ is not explored.

Details on radar elevation ambiguity: Millimeter-wave radar typically suffers from high noise and severe elevation ambiguity. While the paper describes using learnable prototypes to filter outliers, it would be beneficial to provide more concrete details or visualizations showing how the model explicitly handles vertical ambiguity during the fusion step.

Lack of latency and parameter comparisons: Although the paper qualitatively argues that predicting $N+1$ coefficients adds negligible computational overhead, a quantitative table comparing the parameter count, GFLOPs, and runtime/inference speed against the baselines would make the efficiency claims stronger.

strengths: Elegant and well-motivated formulation: Proposing to model scale alignment as a polynomial fitting problem to correct non-uniform misalignments from monocular depth estimation (MDE) is simple, elegant, and theoretically sound.

Effective monotonicity regularization: The inclusion of a first-derivative loss to enforce monotonicity (making the mapping function roughly isotonic) successfully mitigates the standard oscillation issues associated with high-degree polynomial fitting.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The proposed method is validated on three distinct and diverse autonomous driving datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft), where it consistently achieves substantial and state-of-the-art performance improvements (e.g., reducing MAE by up to 54.6%).

Detailed analysis and ablation: The paper provides thorough ablation studies regarding different MDE backbones, polynomial degrees, and core module designs (learnable prototypes and cross-modality attention), offering useful insights into how the system behaves under different choices.
weaknesses: Soft vs. strict monotonicity constraints: The first-derivative regularization (Eq. 8) is a soft L1 loss term. While it successfully regularizes the training, it does not mathematically guarantee strict monotonicity everywhere. It would be interesting to discuss if depth ordering inversion ever occurs in practice, and whether stricter constraint formulations (e.g., enforcing positive coefficients or utilizing bounded activation functions) were explored.

Reliance on 1D transformation mapping: Because the polynomial transformation is applied pixel-wise ($z \to \hat{d}$), it cannot correct internal spatial topological errors made by the MDE model (e.g., if the MDE model completely misses a boundary or hallucinates an object structure). Highlighting these limitations under failure cases of the MDE backbones would make the paper more comprehensive.

strengths: Elegant and novel formulation: Instead of treating scale ambiguity as a simple global linear scale-and-shift or relying on heavy dense depth completion architectures, this work frames radar-guided depth estimation as a scene-fitting polynomial transformation problem.

Well-motivated mathematical constraints: The introduction of the first-derivative regularization term ($||1 - d\hat{d}/dz||_1$) is theoretically sound. It effectively prevents the polynomial from oscillating or violating local depth monotonicity, which is a common failure mode for high-degree polynomial fitting.

Consistent and significant performance gains: PolyRad achieves outstanding improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple challenging automotive datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft), demonstrating its efficacy and robustness.

Great compatibility and flexibility: The method is shown to consistently improve depth estimation across various MDE backbones (e.g., DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, UniDepth), proving its value as a general-purpose plug-and-play adapter.

High-quality presentation: The paper is exceptionally well-written, with intuitive geometric explanations, clear figures (especially Figures 1 and 4 illustrating the need for inflection points), and comprehensive ablation studies.
weaknesses: Spatially-invariant transformation limitation: The polynomial transformation $\hat{d} = f(z)$ is spatially invariant, meaning pixels with the same predicted MDE depth $z$ will always map to the same metric depth $\hat{d}$. If the initial MDE model has spatially inconsistent errors (e.g., underestimating depth on the left side but overestimating it on the right side of the same image), this global polynomial fitting cannot resolve the spatial misalignment. This limitation should be explicitly discussed.

Robustness to extreme radar noise: While the paper mentions that learnable prototypes help mitigate outliers compared to direct pooling, it lacks a dedicated quantitative stress-test showing how performance degrades under varying degrees of radar noise, multipath reflections, or extreme clutter.

strengths: Strong Motivation & Theoretical Grounding: The paper challenges the traditional global affine transformation (scale-and-shift) assumption used for MDE scale alignment. It successfully proves and demonstrates that global affine corrections fail when multiple objects are misaligned relative to each other, and elegantly addresses this using polynomial fitting.

Well-designed and Novel Methodology: The introduction of a polynomial fitting framework for transforming scaleless depth to metric depth is highly original in this domain. The proposed first-derivative monotonicity regularization is a simple yet highly effective mechanism to prevent high-degree polynomial oscillations and preserve local relative structure.

State-of-the-Art Performance: Evaluating on three challenging benchmarks (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft), the proposed POLAR method demonstrates substantial performance gains, outperforming recent state-of-the-art methods like TacoDepth and RadarCam-Depth by a large margin (e.g., on ZJU dataset).

Excellent Computational Efficiency: In addition to being more accurate, POLAR is highly efficient, achieving 40.3 FPS (24.81 ms) and a 39.5% reduction in GFLOPs compared to the previous state-of-the-art, making it highly practical for real-world deployment.

Thorough and Clear Analysis: The paper is exceptionally well-written. The inclusion of extensive comparative studies (testing different MDE backbones), sensitivity analyses (varying polynomial degrees), ablation studies, zero-shot generalization tests, and robustness to reduced radar point density makes the evaluation highly robust.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter Tuning: The choice of the optimal polynomial degree (N) is treated as a hyperparameter that must be tuned (empirically found to be 8). Although analyzed, it would be beneficial to discuss how sensitive this choice is to different camera focal lengths or extreme depth ranges.

Dependence on MDE Structural Quality: Since the method operates by mapping the input MDE depth values through a 1D function, it is inherently unable to correct major structural or topological errors in the original MDE prediction (e.g., if an object is completely merged into the background in the MDE map). A discussion on this fundamental limitation of the fitting formulation would add completeness.

Monotonicity Loss Trade-off: The monotonicity loss encourages the first derivative to remain close to 1. While this prevents overfitting and unstable oscillations, it might also over-constrain the model in scenarios where the MDE model's relative scale is highly non-linear or distorted. Some discussion on this trade-off would be insightful.

strengths: Elegant and theoretically grounded motivation: The paper successfully challenges the common assumption that MDE scale misalignment is purely linear (affine). It proves theoretically and empirically that a global scale-and-shift cannot resolve multi-object relative depth discrepancies, and introduces polynomial fitting to address this.

Effective Regularization Design: Enforcing monotonicity through a first-derivative regularization term is a clever way to constrain the high-degree polynomial function space. This prevents depth-order reversal and keeps the local structural quality of MDE predictions intact.

State-of-the-Art Performance: POLAR demonstrates massive improvements over existing radar-camera depth estimation methods on three benchmarks (nuScenes, ZJU, and View-of-Delft), reducing MAE and RMSE substantially.

High Computational Efficiency: Since the network only predicts a small number of global polynomial coefficients rather than dense depth maps, it enjoys extremely fast training, ultra-low GFLOPs, and real-time inference (over 40 fps), making it highly practical for real-world deployment.

Thorough Evaluation and Ablations: The paper provides extensive supplementary results, including comparisons across multiple MDE backbones, sensitivity analysis of the polynomial degree, zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation, and robustness to reduced radar point densities.
weaknesses: Numerical Stability with High-Degree Polynomials: Computing powers of depth up to $N=8$ can easily lead to numerical instability or exploding gradients if the input depth values $z$ are large. The paper would benefit from a discussion on how depth maps are normalized/scaled before being fed into the polynomial equation.

Lack of Comparison with Local Affine Methods: The primary comparison is against a global scale-and-shift. However, some depth completion methods predict spatially-varying (pixel-wise or region-wise) affine parameters. A discussion or comparison with such local scaling baselines would further clarify the advantages of global polynomial fitting.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity: The optimal polynomial degree $N$ is highly dataset-dependent and needs careful tuning (e.g., $N=8$ works best, but $N=10$ degrades performance due to oscillations). A more adaptive mechanism to regularize higher-order coefficients (e.g., L1 regularization on coefficients) could have been explored to automate this choice.

strengths: The paper is grounded in a strong and intuitive geometric insight: pretrained monocular depth estimation (MDE) models often predict reasonable local object structures but misalign relative depths across different regions, which cannot be corrected by a global affine (scale-and-shift) transformation.

Framing radar-camera depth estimation as a polynomial fitting problem is highly elegant and well-suited to the extreme sparsity and noise of radar data, avoiding the ill-posedness of standard dense depth completion methods.

The introduction of a first-derivative monotonicity constraint is a clever way to stabilize high-degree polynomial fitting, effectively preventing depth inversions and maintaining the reliable ordinal relationships of the MDE model.

The proposed method shows outstanding empirical performance, outperforming recent state-of-the-art methods (such as GET-UP, RadarCam-Depth, and TacoDepth) on three challenging datasets (nuScenes, ZJU, and View-of-Delft).
POLAR achieves superior computational efficiency, running in real-time at over 40 fps with significantly fewer GFLOPs and shorter training times than existing dense fusion architectures.

The paper is exceptionally well-written, containing thorough mathematical justification, comprehensive ablation studies, and robust qualitative/quantitative comparisons in both the main text and the appendix.
weaknesses: The predicted polynomial coefficients are applied globally to the entire image. If the MDE model's distortion is spatially non-uniform across coordinates (e.g., depth distortion on the left side of the camera frame is different from the right side), a single global polynomial transformation cannot correct it.

The monotonicity loss term in Eq. 6 penalizes the deviation of the first derivative from 1 (i.e., encouraging $\frac{d\hat{d}}{dz} \approx 1$). This might be overly restrictive as it encourages the transformation to remain near identity, potentially limiting the polynomial's capacity to make necessary non-linear scale adjustments. A one-sided constraint (e.g., penalizing only negative derivatives) could provide more flexibility.

The optimal polynomial degree $N$ is a sensitive hyperparameter that varies by dataset. As shown in the sensitivity analysis, choosing an incorrect $N$ can lead to either underfitting or performance degradation due to oscillations.
